newsitem.title: USA: Dollar rebounds sharply against yen, mark.
newsitem.headline: Dollar rebounds sharply against yen, mark.

text.p: The dollar rose sharply on Wednesday in a rebound from the previous day's losses, boosted by a mixed Japanese economic report and reports suggesting the Federal Reserve could push up U.S. interest rates again soon.
Expectations of a strong Tankan report -- the Bank of Japan's quarterly reading on corporate sentiment -- had depressed the dollar against the Japanese yen on Tuesday.
While the report did show some improvement in the mood of Japan's corporations when it was released on Wednesday, it also highlighted insecurity about the future, leading to sales of yen.
"The market was looking for more strength in the Tankan report than they got," said Dominick Presa, chief dealer of foreign exchange at Dresdner Bank.
The key index rose to plus two in March from minus three in the previous survey last November, the first positive reading since November 1991.
But this strength contrasted sharply whith the mood among non-manufacturers, whose index plunged beyond most expectations to minus six from zero in November.
The dollar ended the day at 123.24 yen, up from 121.73 yen late Tuesday.
Against the German mark, the dollar rose to 1.6755 from 1.6663 late Tuesday and above Monday's close of 1.6750.
Also helping the dollar, dealers said, were several news reports which raised the possibility of more interest rate hikes from the Fed.

An article in the Washington Post quoted Fed Governor Laurence Meyer as saying the U.S. economy was "really strong" and suggested that recent data pointed to another credit tightening from the central bank next month.
A newswire report quoting unnamed Fed sources also raised the prospect for further Fed rate rises on Wednesday.
Higher U.S. interest rates tend to make dollar assets comparatively more attractive.
The market largely ignored comments by prominent U.S. economist Fred Bergsten that by highlighting trade issues with Japan, the Treasury Department was implicitly calling for a stronger yen.
On Tuesday and Wednesday, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said a renewed rise in Japan's trade surplus could cause friction between Japan and the United States.
"Bergsten's and Rubin's comments didn't even budge the dollar," said Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"I think the market got caught leaning the wrong way," after Tuesday's dollar sell-off, Chandler added.
In other trade on Wednesday, the dollar ended modestly higher at 1.4420 Swiss francs against 1.4415 late Tuesday.
The British pound fell to $1.6440 from $1.6530 and the dollar dropped to Canadian $1.3858 from C$1.3892.
